artworks.title: Hermes and Herse
artworks.description: Attic red-figure cup (Louvre G494): Hermes pursues Herse, Cecrops’ daughter, in a chase painted for a drinking party. The vase is among the earliest clear images of the Athenian princess whom Ovid would later make Mercury’s desire — and Aglauros’ fatal envy.

artworks.title: Lekythos with Hermes and Herse
artworks.description: White-ground lekythos (Museo Arqueológico Nacional, Madrid): Hermes and Herse meet in a spare funerary palette. The Attic oil-flask keeps Cecrops’ daughter in the same visual company as her sisters — a private, named encounter before the Roman poets thickened the jealousy plot.

artworks.title: Mercury, Herse, and Aglaurus
artworks.description: Lagrenée’s Nationalmuseum canvas stages Ovid’s triangle: Mercury at the threshold, Herse the prize, Aglauros the envious sister who will turn to stone. French neoclassical polish makes the Cecropid household a moral tableau of desire blocked by jealousy.

artworks.title: Mercury, Herse, and Aglauros
artworks.description: Poussin’s ENSBA drawing compresses Metamorphoses II into a Roman doorway drama — Mercury, Herse, and the sister who bars the way. It is the classical French reading of Cecrops’ daughter as the beloved whom envy cannot keep from the messenger god.

artworks.title: The Daughters of Cecrops Finding the Child Erichthonius
artworks.description: Jordaens’ Antwerp canvas (and its Wikipedia dossier) shows Herse with Aglauros and Pandrosos opening Athena’s chest — the other Cecropid myth that keeps her among Athens’ founding sisters. Baroque flesh and shock fix the three princesses at the moment curiosity dooms them.

popCulture.title: Metamorphoses II (Mercury and Herse)
popCulture.creator: Ovid
popCulture.description: Ovid’s Mercury-and-Herse episode — Aglauros turned to stone for envy — is the Latin narrative that made Cecrops’ daughter a staple of early-modern painting.
